speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: asked the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry (a) what is the policy basis for providing the Electric Vehicle Early Adoption Incentive (EEAI) but declining equivalent capital subsidies for residential rooftop solar panel installation; (b) what are the (i) take-up rates of the EEAI and (ii) proportion of private households that have installed solar panels; and (c) whether the Ministry will introduce comparable capital grants or property tax rebates for residential solar panels.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling
text: asked the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Trade and Industry in view of the energy crisis, whether the Government will consider (i) mandating the installation of solar panels for all new buildings and estates and (ii) providing greater incentives for existing building owners to install solar panels.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: This corresponds to about 8% of all private residential buildings.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: The growth in solar deployment has been driven by favourable economics.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Solar panel costs have come down over the years and the payback period for rooftop solar can be five years or even less.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: The Government has also introduced measures that can help to further reduce the payback period for eligible building owners.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: For example, eligible private buildings can tap on the Green Mark Incentive Scheme for Existing Buildings 2.0, which helps building owners lower the upfront cost of energy improvement works, such as solar panel installation.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Some jurisdictions have made it mandatory for new buildings to install solar panels.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: In Singapore, we have no plans at this stage to mandate solar panel installation on buildings because some building owners may prioritise other rooftop uses, such as greenery, or their rooftops may not be suited to solar installation due to factors, such as shading from neighbouring tall buildings.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: The Government strongly encourages all building owners to install solar panels if this is feasible.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: With ongoing global uncertainty in energy prices, solar installation can provide building owners with savings and greater predictability on their electricity bills while contributing to Singapore's overall energy resilience.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: In recent weeks, some solar vendors locally have reported an increase in interest in solar panels among private building owners.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: This could be partly because of the recent increase in the regulated tariff for electricity and also perhaps some anticipation of further increase in the tariff.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: For building owners who may be concerned about the costs of installing solar panels, some solar vendors offer “rent-to-own” or “solar leasing” models that allow building owners to enjoy the benefits of solar installation with little to no upfront cost.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Mr Kenneth Tiong has asked on the Electric Vehicle Early Adoption Incentive (EEAI).

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: The EEAI was implemented in January 2021 to encourage the early adoption of electric vehicles (EVs) by reducing the gap in total upfront cost between an EV and equivalent internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicle.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: The EEAI parameters have tapered with narrowing upfront costs capped over the years and will cease from 1 January 2027.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: As of March 2026, more than 55,000 electric cars and taxis have benefited from the EEAI.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: The Government will continue to push for solar deployment in Singapore and will consider further measures if necessary to accelerate solar adoption in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Residential rooftop solar generates clean energy and reduces household dependence on imported natural gas and provides a hedge against energy price shocks – benefits that EVs, which add demand to the same gas-dependent grid, do not provide.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I note that the Minister of State has mentioned the Green Mark scheme.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Despite the Green Mark scheme, 92% of eligible rooftops are still without solar panels.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: So, my first supplementary question is, why does she believe that that is currently the case?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: And my second supplementary question is, would the Ministry consider providing more of the same type of upfront support available for EV purchases to accelerate residential solar adoption?

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: So, if you compare it with a few years ago, there was hesitancy in private building owners to adopt solar deployment, but now we are, indeed, seeing a much higher interest among private building owners, including residential properties.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: And we believe that the economics will drive faster adoption.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Having said that, we will monitor closely the rate of adoption and the Government is prepared to consider additional measures, if necessary.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: On the point about EEAI, actually EEAI works in a certain way.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: It assumes that the consumer wants to buy a vehicle and is choosing between different types of vehicles.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: And in this case, the EEAI nudges the consumer to consider an EV, even though an EV could be more costly than an ICE vehicle.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: But for building owners, here, we are talking about catalysing a purchase, a new purchase.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: It is not just about whether there is an incentive from the Government.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: But some of the private residential building owners have also expressed some other considerations.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: For example, some are concerned about whether it will affect the integrity of the waterproofing for the roof.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Others have also said that they are unsure about the reliability of the solar panel installation vendors.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: And of course, there are some building owners who prefer to keep their rooftops for other purposes and preferring not to install solar panels.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Even if you have a grant, it may not nudge them to go for the purchase.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: I think it is important that we understand the issue closely and look at what it takes for us to be able to effectively nudge private building owners to go towards solar installation.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: First, as a small country that cannot take energy security for granted, could the Minister of State share whether Singapore may increasingly move towards designing future developments and estates to be more solar ready from the outset, so that we strengthen our long-term resilience rather than rely on retrofitting later on?

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Second, could the Minister of State also elaborate on whether there are opportunities for closer collaboration and coordination across agencies involved in energy planning, urban development and building design, so that solar deployment can be integrated more systematically upstream in future developments?

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: And third, as Singapore scales up solar deployment over time, how is the Ministry strengthening our local ecosystem of manpower, technical expertise and supply resilience to support this transition in a sustainable and long-term fashion?

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Indeed, the Government agencies are working closely together to look at how we can make solar installation in Singapore easier and more cost-effective for the building owners.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: New buildings are required to meet standards under the Building and Construction Authority's (BCA's) Code for Environmental Sustainability of Buildings, with solar being recognised as one of the acceptable carbon-reduction measures under the Code.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Solar installation is certainly one of the means.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: There are also other things that building designs can take into account, where it is more practical, for example, energy consumption, the building design and ventilation.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: There are several things that building owners can adopt and not be limited to just solar.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Of course, we believe that solar, because of its cost effectiveness, going forward, there will be more adopters of this technology.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: We will continue to push the boundaries whenever possible and to explore more innovative solar deployments in Singapore, such as at car parks and bridges and even in between buildings.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: I also want to highlight another example of how our agencies are working together to simplify regulations to make it easier to install solar panels.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: Last year, the Singapore Civil Defence Force reviewed the fire safety requirement for one-hour fire separation for roof-mounted solar panel installations.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: So, it is both regulatory codes and also review of existing regulations for us to move both new buildings and existing buildings toward higher adoption of solar as well as other environment sustainability measures.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: On the third question on strengthening our local ecosystem, that is a really good question.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: We have been working on that for a long time with our institutes of higher learning (IHLs), both for pre-employment training for the graduates as well as for continuing education and training for adults who have graduated from our IHLs.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: There is a skills framework for energy and power that is developed jointly by the Government, industry, the unions and the IHLs.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Second, for all private property owners, to develop a simple starter kit with standard templates on procurement; financing option, such as power purchase agreements; also matters on maintenance, roles and responsibilities of vendors and warrantees; and also, importantly, provide a white list of vendors so that private property owners will have the confidence to engage vendors.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: This will be helpful and we are awaiting BCA's completion of this review.

speaker: Ms Gan Siow Huang
text: On the suggestion to have a starter kit for private property owners, especially residential owners, that is a very good idea.
